title: T/F/NI + Vocabulary: The Mall That Wanted to Be a Town (poziom wojewodzki)

tasks.instruction: Przeczytaj ponizszy tekst. Zdecyduj, ktore zdania (1.1.–1.5.) sa zgodne z trescia tekstu (T – True), ktore sa niezgodne (F – False), a ktore zawieraja informacje niepodane w tekscie (NI – No Information). Nastepnie znajdz w tekscie wyrazy lub wyrazenia, ktore odpowiadaja definicjom podanym w punktach 1.6.–1.10. Wymagana jest calkowita poprawnosc ortograficzna odpowiedzi.
tasks.text:
THE MALL THAT WANTED TO BE A TOWN

Victor Gruen, the architect usually credited with inventing the shopping mall, spent the last part of his life saying that he wanted nothing to do with it. He had arrived in the United States from Vienna in 1938 with, by his own account, eight dollars and no English, and he brought with him a European idea of what a town centre was: a covered, walkable place with shops, certainly, but also a library, a clinic, apartments and a school. His first great commission, opened in Minnesota in 1956, delivered the covered walkable part beautifully. The developers were markedly less enthusiastic about the school.

What was built instead, thousands of times over the following three decades, was the retail half of the idea surrounded by an ocean of parking. It suited the country it was built in. Land outside the cities was cheap, petrol was cheaper, and a generation was moving out to the suburbs and taking its spending with it. By 1990 the United States had more shopping centre floor space for each of its citizens than any other nation on earth, and the gap was not a narrow one.

The decline, when it came, is usually blamed entirely on the internet, which is at best half the story. American developers had already built far more retail space than the population could support; the industry was overextended before online shopping amounted to a meaningful share of anything. What the internet removed was the margin for error. The weakest malls - the ones with the wrong tenants, in the wrong suburbs, with roofs coming to the end of their lives - emptied first, and the emptying has a momentum to it, because shoppers stop coming to a building where half the units are papered over, which empties the other half.

The abandoned ones have acquired a strange second existence online, photographed by enthusiasts who trade pictures of dead escalators and fountains full of dust. Those photographs are seductive and slightly misleading, because the commoner fate of a failing mall is not abandonment but conversion. Several have become medical centres, on the reasoning that a building with wide corridors, plentiful parking and a bus route already outside makes a perfectly good clinic. Others have been turned into offices, into distribution warehouses for the very companies that undermined them, into churches and schools, and in a handful of cases into the mixed districts of housing and shops that Gruen wanted in the first place.

His own disappointment is well recorded, largely because he recorded it himself. In a lecture given late in life he refused, as he put it, to pay alimony for the developments that had been built in his name - a line quoted so often since that it has almost come loose from him. What angered him was not the buildings but what grew up around them. He had imagined the mall as the dense heart of a planned community, with housing pressing right up against it; what each one produced instead was a ring of car parks, access roads and identical retail strips, pushing the town further apart rather than drawing it together. The phrase Gruen transfer, invented by other people for the moment when a shopper loses track of what they came in for, would have annoyed him for a quite different reason: he had never intended the place to be a trap.

Meanwhile the format he is blamed for is doing well in other places. New malls continue to open across Asia and the Gulf, where air conditioning is not a luxury and the building functions, much as Gruen argued it should, as the public space a hot city otherwise lacks. Teenagers meet there because there is nowhere else to meet; families walk there in the evening. The building type he disowned is thriving, in other words, in more or less the form he originally described - just not on the continent that made it famous.

items.statement: Gruen's original plan for the shopping centre included facilities that were not shops.
items.explanation: TRUE - He wanted 'a library, a clinic, apartments and a school' alongside the shops.

items.statement: The decline of the American mall can be explained entirely by the growth of online shopping.
items.explanation: FALSE - Blaming the internet is 'at best half the story'; the industry 'was overextended' before online shopping mattered.

items.statement: Failing American malls are more often left empty than put to a new use.
items.explanation: FALSE - 'The commoner fate of a failing mall is not abandonment but conversion' into clinics, offices, warehouses and schools.

items.statement: Gruen went back to live in Europe after he stopped practising as an architect.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION - The text records his arrival in America in 1938 and his later opinions, but says nothing about where he spent his final years.

items.statement: Shopping centres in the Gulf attract more visitors at weekends than during the week.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION - The text says teenagers and families use them, but never compares one day with another.
